prompt: What separates a framework from a library, in the sense the lesson uses?

choices.text: A framework is larger and has more modules
choices.why: Size decides nothing: desk.py is a framework of a dozen lines.

choices.text: A framework calls you; you call a library
choices.why: Right. Who holds the loop is the whole difference.

choices.text: A library has to be installed, while a framework ships with the language
choices.why: unittest ships with Python and is a framework; textwrap ships with it too and is a library.

choices.text: A framework only exists for web applications
choices.why: unittest and tkinter are frameworks with no web in them.

prompt: In desk.py, the request to renew Vidas Secas was skipped. Which code made that decision?

choices.text: The lend handler, which saw a title it did not expect
choices.why: lend was never called for that request; no handler was registered for renew.

choices.text: Python, because the dictionary lookup raised an error
choices.why: Desk.run uses get, which returns None instead of raising; the skip is a branch in run.

choices.text: Desk.run, the loop of the framework
choices.why: Right. The framework owns the loop, so it decides what happens to a request nobody handles.

prompt: "Don't call us, we'll call you" is the old name for inversion of control: the ___ principle.
Why does OverdueNotices receive a Clock instead of calling date.today() itself?

choices.text: date.today() is slow, and a clock object caches the answer
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; FixedClock exists so the day can be chosen.

choices.text: So the caller decides which day it is
choices.why: Right. "What day is it" is a dependency, and the most often forgotten one.

choices.text: Python forbids calling date.today() inside a method
choices.why: It allows it; the first draft did exactly that, and it worked until somebody needed 20 March.

choices.text: Every class must take a clock, as a rule of SOLID
choices.why: No principle says so; only classes whose behaviour depends on the date need one.

prompt: OverdueNotices is built with FixedClock(date(2026, 3, 20)). A loan was due on 9 March 2026. What fine, in cents, does its notice quote?
hint: 50 cents for each day after the due date.

prompt: A class you are reviewing takes seven collaborators in its constructor. What does the lesson read into that?

choices.text: Constructor injection has hit its limit and a container is needed
choices.why: A container would hide the seven, not remove them; the class would still do seven things.

choices.text: Half of them should move to setters so the constructor reads shorter
choices.why: That only hides them and loses the guarantee that each one is present.

choices.text: The class is probably doing several jobs, and the long list is just being honest about it
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3's single responsibility principle is the conversation to have about it.

prompt: Match each form of injection to the moment a missing dependency is noticed.

pairs.right: at the first use, possibly much later
at the call that should have passed it

prompt: In forms.py, Reminder() succeeded and the first remind() failed with 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'send'. What does that show?

choices.text: Setter injection lets an object exist without what it needs
choices.why: Right. Between construction and the assignment the object is broken, and nothing says so until it is used.

choices.text: PrintNotifier has a bug in its send method
choices.why: PrintNotifier was never reached; the attribute was still None.

choices.text: Python cannot assign an attribute after an object is built, so the notifier is lost
choices.why: It can; the third line of output came from a Reminder whose notifier was assigned afterwards.

prompt: The desk prints a receipt for one member and texts it to the next, using the same Receipt object. Which form fits?

choices.text: Constructor injection, with one Receipt per channel kept for the day
choices.why: It works, but it builds objects to carry a choice that changes with every call.

choices.text: Method injection
choices.why: Right. The dependency changes from call to call, so each call passes it.

choices.text: A service locator that the desk updates before each receipt
choices.why: That is global state changing under the receipt, and the call no longer shows which channel it uses.

choices.text: Setter injection, setting the notifier before every receipt
choices.why: Possible, and one forgotten assignment sends a receipt down the previous member's channel.

prompt: What is the composition root of a program?

choices.text: The base class every service of the program inherits its wiring from
choices.why: Nothing inherits from it; it is the place where objects are built and connected.

choices.text: The place near the entry point that builds and wires every object
choices.why: Right. In main.py it is build.

choices.text: The top directory of the repository, where main.py is kept
choices.why: It is code, not a folder: the root of the object graph.

prompt: A colleague adds a helper inside OverdueNotices that writes SmsNotifier() for urgent notices. What has changed?

choices.text: Nothing important, since SmsNotifier still matches the Notifier protocol
choices.why: Matching the protocol is not the issue; the job now chooses a concrete class, which only main.py was meant to do.

choices.text: A choice that belonged to the composition root is back inside the job
choices.why: Right. Changing how urgent notices go out now means finding that helper.

choices.text: The program will no longer run, because OverdueNotices may not import anything
choices.why: It still runs; the cost is in design, and it shows the day somebody wants e-mail instead.

choices.text: The job becomes a service locator
choices.why: Nothing is fetched from a registry; the class is constructed directly, which is the original problem.

prompt: Put what happens when main.py runs in order.
items: Read the channel from the arguments and LIBRARY_TODAY from the environment
Build the store, the notifier and the clock
Call send_all and print how many were sent
trap: Building the job before its collaborators is impossible with constructor injection: it needs them as arguments.

prompt: How does the container in container.py know that OverdueNotices needs a Clock?

choices.text: Clock was registered before OverdueNotices
choices.why: Order of registration plays no part; the bare container refused even though everything else was registered.

choices.text: It reads the type hints on __init__
choices.why: Right. get_type_hints is the autowiring; without the hints it would know nothing.

choices.text: It calls the constructor with no arguments and studies the error it gets back
choices.why: It never calls a constructor without arguments; it resolves every hinted parameter first.

choices.text: OverdueNotices registers its own needs when it is imported
choices.why: OverdueNotices knows nothing about the container, and that is what keeps it reusable.

prompt: wired.py printed same notifier: True and same clock: False. Why the difference?

choices.text: A clock holds a date, and objects holding dates are always rebuilt
choices.why: The container knows nothing about dates; it follows what was registered.

choices.text: The clock was registered as a lambda, and lambdas cannot be compared with is
choices.why: The comparison is between the objects resolve returned, and any two objects can be compared with is.

choices.text: Only the notifier was registered with shared=True
choices.why: Right. That is a lifetime: one shared instance, or a new one per request.

prompt: A command-line tool of twelve classes is wired by hand in main. A teammate proposes adding a container. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Keep the hand wiring; at this size a container costs more than it saves
choices.why: Right. The trade pays when the wiring is large, repetitive or per request, and none of that is true here.

choices.text: Add it, because constructor injection does not work without one
choices.why: main.py injects by hand and works; the container automates what build already does.

choices.text: Add it, since a container finds missing dependencies before the program even starts
choices.why: A runtime container finds them at resolve; hand wiring in main fails at least as early.

prompt: Injection and a service locator both keep SmtpNotifier() out of the job. What is the difference?

choices.text: A locator is faster, because nothing has to be passed through every constructor on the way
choices.why: Passing an argument costs nothing worth measuring; the difference is in what a reader and a test can see.

choices.text: With injection the object is handed its collaborators; with a locator it fetches them
choices.why: Right. The direction is the difference, and it decides whether the constructor tells the truth.

choices.text: A locator works with protocols, and injection with concrete classes
choices.why: Both work with either; OverdueNotices is injected with protocols.

prompt: A team imports its container into every class and calls container.resolve(Notifier) inside methods. What have they built?

choices.text: Dependency injection, since a container is doing the work
choices.why: A container used this way is asked from inside, which is fetching, not being handed.

choices.text: A composition root spread across the files
choices.why: A root is one place by definition; spread out, it is the scattering the root exists to end.

choices.text: A service locator, whatever the container is called
choices.why: Right. The tool is the same; asking it from inside methods makes it a locator.

choices.text: Inversion of control, because no class constructs its own notifier
choices.why: Each class still decides when to get its notifier and from where; nothing is handed to it.

prompt: Which of these does the service locator in locator.py hide or cause? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The constructor claims the class needs nothing
choices.why: Right. LocatedNotices() takes no arguments and uses three services.

choices.text: A missing clock is found inside the loop rather than at construction
choices.why: Right. The object was built and announced before the KeyError.

choices.text: One test's fake can leak into the next test
choices.why: Right. The registry is global, so what one test provides stays for the next.

choices.text: The job sends notices to the wrong members
choices.why: The rule is the same as in OverdueNotices; what changed is how the collaborators arrive.

prompt: Why does test_overdue.py need no unittest.mock.patch at all?

choices.text: Because unittest refuses patches in a class that has setUp
choices.why: setUp and patch work together fine; there is simply nothing to patch.

choices.text: The job is handed its clock and notifier, so the test hands it fakes
choices.why: Right. A class that builds nothing has nothing to reach into.

choices.text: PrintNotifier never sends anything real, so it needs no replacing
choices.why: The test does not use PrintNotifier at all; it passes a RecordingNotifier.

prompt: A test patches "overdue_draft.SmtpNotifier". The job is then moved to a file called jobs.py and the test is left alone. What happens?

choices.text: Python updates the patch target to follow the moved class
choices.why: A patch target is a string; nothing rewrites it.

choices.text: The patch misses, and the real mail server is called
choices.why: Right. The patch was coupled to an import name, not to what the job needs.

choices.text: The test keeps working exactly as before
choices.why: jobs.py looks up its own SmtpNotifier; the patch replaced the name in the old module.

choices.text: Every test in the file fails to import
choices.why: Only the moved job changes; whether the test notices at all is the danger.

prompt: In test_overdue.py, Loan and ListedLoans are the real classes. Why are they not faked?

choices.text: They are fast, deterministic and ours, so faking them would test nothing
choices.why: Right. Fake what is slow, non-deterministic or outside the process.

choices.text: A frozen dataclass cannot be replaced by a double
choices.why: It could; any object with the same fields would do. It is just pointless.

choices.text: Faking every collaborator is the rule, and these two were forgotten
choices.why: A test that fakes everything checks only call order and breaks on every refactor.

prompt: Match each line of this lesson's code to the idea it shows.
Deep inside a mailer class, a method reads os.environ["SMTP_HOST"] and builds a connection. Which change does this lesson point to?

choices.text: Register the host in a global Services registry so every class can read it
choices.why: That swaps one hidden dependency for another; the method would still fetch.

choices.text: Read the variable in a setter that the mailer calls on itself
choices.why: The class would still decide where its configuration comes from.

choices.text: Read it in main and pass the connection in
choices.why: Right. Configuration is read once, near the entry point, and the class receives what it needs.

prompt: A test passes when run alone and fails when run after another test in the same file. Which design from this lesson is the usual suspect?

choices.text: Constructor injection, because setUp builds a new object each time
choices.why: A fresh object per test is what keeps tests independent.

choices.text: A service locator, whose global registry keeps what the first test provided
choices.why: Right. Order-dependent tests are the signature of shared global state.

choices.text: Method injection, which passes a different notifier on every call
choices.why: Each call names its notifier, so nothing carries over between tests.

choices.text: A composition root, since main.py runs before the tests
choices.why: The tests never import main.py; the root is not part of what is tested.
